title: Lululemon: The 15-Minute Thesis
snippet: Our 40-minute Deep Dive, condensed to the numbers, moat, risks, valuation, investment case and our verdict. Is Michael Burry right about his largest bet?
content_html:
What Does the Company Do?

Lululemon is a brand of premium athletic-apparel that designes technical wear (known especially for their leggings). The company is known for outsourcing the production and selling the products mainly via its own stores and website. This has historically produced a highly profitable direct-to-consumer model.

But its moat is rather debatable and it hinges on “mind share” and loyalty of its customers. There are zero switching costs, and consumers that were buying Lululemon yesterday, can go today for Alo, Vuori or cheaper dupes with no friction whatsover.

The seemingly fragile moat is even under more pressure after Q2 2026, where revenue fell 4%, Americas comparable sales dropped 12%, margins shrank, and legging sales reportedly fell 20%.

The stock has plummeted and is definitely Hated. However, is it a Hated Moat?

Why Is It Hated?

has gone from a premium compounder to potentially being a value trap. The stock is down more than 50% YTD as its North American business shrinks, leggings weaken, and Alo and Vuori gain share. Slower reactions to changing trends and product missteps have raised questions and fears of a structural problem in the brand, and deservingly so. The bull argument of the weaker broad sector and cycle phase doesn’t hold up, since competition is gaining market share and grow revenue.

On the other side, LULU’s FY2026 guidance has been cut twice, with revenue now expected to fall 5-7% and Q3 down 10-11%. With margins under pressure and a new CEO inheriting this mess, investors no longer know whether LULU is a turnaround story, or a fading brand story whose moat was temporarily overstated due to cultural hype. And the market Hates uncertainty.

Share

Competitive Moat & Peer Comparison

It’d be unfair to claim LULU doesn’t have any moat at all. It does, altough it’s a soft/fragile one, depending on personal brand preference and the mentioned “mind share”, while the fact remains that there’s zero friction in switching to competition.

The strength of the moat comes from years of expertise in fabrics, fit and construction. There are also roughly 825 LULU stores worldwide that serve as marketing and community hubs. In the recent years, Lululemon has become the default premium choice for affluent, wellness-focused consumers willing to pay $100+ for technical apparel. The problem also is, this default choice might not be as obvious anymore. And (yet) another problem is that investors are not willing to pay $100+ for the stock right now.

We believe it’s easier to overstate the moat itself than it is to defend it. We have manufacturing that’s outsourced and majority of the technology is unpatented here. The competitors use the same global supply chain. If a dupe feels 80% or 90% the same as original, LULU must justify the price in other way (brand, design alone,…).

We believe the mentioned makes traffic, conversion and full-price demand key moat metrics. And all of those are weakinging… Margins are also under pressure, with more markdowns. For a preference-based moat, every purchase of product is a vote for that moat. Right now, Lululemon appears to be winning fewer of them.

Share

The Competition

More credible rivals than Nike or adidas are trying to eat Lulu’s lunch. Alo targets the very same type of affluent customer, while Vuori is expanding horizonatally (men, women, retail).

Also important to note, as we mentioned above, strong growth of companies like Deckers and On does suggest that recent Lululemon’s weakness is not just cyclical.

The moat still exists, but it’s weakening in North America as traffic, conversion, store productivity and market share decline.

So our Hated Moats question naturally is:

Is this a temporarily wounded brand, or a formerly dominant category leader discovering that its moat was mostly preference in a market that has become crowded, fashionable and easy to copy?

If the answer is the latter, Lululemon can remain an excellent brand and still lose part of the economic advantage that once made it look like an exceptional business.

Recent Stock Performance & Market Sentiment

LULU closed September 10, 2026 at $96.88, down more than 53% YTD, which is a new 8-year low. The main reasons for this are quite understandable, and mostly listed above.

Q2 print deepened the trend of plummeting. EPS was boosted by tariff refunds, while FY2026 revenue guidance fell to $10.35-10.50B and EPS to $9.48-9.73. Shares dropped 17% on the day with investors questioning brand relevance, its moat, market-share losses and the return of 20%+ margins. Bears see a fading compounder while bulls (including Michael Burry) see a debt-free global brand with excellent balance sheet trading near 10x depressed earnings.

So the question is obvious - has the stock fallen further (and quicker) than Lululemon’s long-term earnings power?

Fundamental Analysis

Lululemon si stil finanically strong, but it’s no loger financially growing. We encourage you to read on, of course, but if you can’t, that one sentence is all you really need to know from this section.

Company’s revenue rose from $4.4B in FY2020 to $11.1B in FY2025, yet growth slowed from 42% in FY2021 to 4.9% in FY2025. FY2026 has now tipped into contraction, with H1 revenue flat and full-year guidance implying a 5-7% decline. No bueno.

The weakness is concentrated where it hurts most, i.e. in the Americas, still roughly two-thirds of sales, while China and other international markets (that were supposed to make up for the declining Americas) are also decelerating. Q2 global comps fell 9%, Americas comps 12%, and management cited weaker traffic, conversion and average order value (i.e., in other words, the most crucial metrics).

Margins are deteriorating, too. FY2025 gross margin fell to 56.6% and operating margin to 19.9%. Q2 looked better largely because tariff refunds boosted margins and if we exclude them, underlying gross and operating margins were roughly 54.9% and 13.2%.

Lululemon does remain highly profitable, but revenue, customer metrics and operating leverage are all moving the wrong way,.

Accounting looks generally clean, but Q2 EPS of $2.92 included $0.86 from tariff refunds and interest. Excluding that benefit, earnings were closer to $2.06, down 34% YoY. FCF was $922M in FY2025, below FY2021 despite much higher revenue. H1 FY2026 improved sharply, though largely due to working-capital swings. SBC remains modest and buybacks are genuinely reducing dilution, which we see as objectively truly positive. Shares outstanding have fallen materially, supporting EPS, although it must be said that the management hasn’t always repurchased stock cheaply.

Lululemon’s balance sheet remains excellent, and it’s the best part about the company, as far as our analysis goes. $1.39B cash, no funded debt, roughly $2.14B working capital and a 2.2x current ratio. The balance sheet points to the fact that the potential turnaround is operational, not financial. LULU isn’t in rush, the company can afford to take its time, and that’s likely one of the main things why Dr. Burry ( ) bet big on the company.

Capital allocation is a topic with more mixed data. LULU spent $3.1B on capex in FY2021-FY2025 and historically earned excellent ROIC, but returns are worsening lately. FY2025 revenue rose $514M while operating income fell $295M, H1 FY2026 revenue was flat and operating income fell 24%. The mentioned bybacks cut share count, but average prices fell from $318 in FY2024 to $237 in FY2025 and $141 in H1 FY2026. With the stock being below $100, that’s some unpleasant downward spiral. As far as capital allocation goes, MIRROR remains the clearest mistake.

Guidance remains the weakest area, and huge part of why we’re sceptical about the company for now. Since March, FY2026 revenue guidance fell from $11.35-$11.50B to $10.35-$10.50B and EPS from $12.10-$12.30 to $9.48-$9.73. Q2 missed guidance and Q3 implies a 10%-11% revenue decline. Excluding the tariff refund, FY2026 EPS is $8.75. Put in simple terms, forecasting credibility deteriorated.

Valuation Overview

At the time of our main analysis, LULU was $100.61. At that price, market cap is roughly $11.1B and EV $9.75B. At 10.5x FY2026 guidance, the stock looks cheap versus its historical premium. But the key question is the durability of earnings. TTM numbers still benefit from stronger FY2025 periods and tariff refunds.

If FY2026 is the trough, and the company will actually start turning around, (sub)-$100 area could be compelling. If margins structurally reset lower and revenue keeps shrinking, the apparent bargain may prove illusory, the knife might keep falling and one might find himself Burryed in a value trap.

Share

Management Quality & Insider Activity

Assessing Lululemon’s management is difficult because we’re seeing a new team as we write. The now former CEO, Calvin McDonald, oversaw enormous growth, international expansion and exceptional margins, but MIRROR was a major capital-allocation mistake. His final years were tarnished by weaker innovation, deteriorating North American comps and rising competition. He’s had enough and left in January 2026.

Incoming CEO Heidi O’Neill has a strong résumé (former Nike executive) but now must prove she can revive the product engine. Her package includes a $1.4M salary, 200% target bonus and $10M of annual equity awards, mostly performance-based. Sweet gig, but for a tough job indeed.

Insider buying is mildly encouraging with André Maestrini buying $495k of shares at $151.02, while director Chip Bergh chipped in with $1.0M at $164.20. Both are underwater quite spectacularly at the time of writing, but meaningful open-market purchases still signal conviction. If insiders liked the stock in $150s-160s, should we love it below $100?

Overall, historical execution was strong but from a certain point on deteriorated sharply. The new leadership now has to earn investor confidence and pull off a successful turnaround story.

Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it.

Risk Factors

Company-Specific Operating Risks

The North American Problem Could Be Structural

This is the main risk according to our research. The bullish interpretation is that Lululemon has a temporary product problem while the bearish one is that it has lost part of the consumer preference that created its moat, i.e. the problem is structural. In a business with no switching costs, customers must be won repeatedly. If Americas comps remain materially negative after the product refresh, the thesis shifts from turnaround to structural share loss.

Product Execution

LULU has seen repeated product misses and for a brand charging premium prices for fit, fabric and technical execution, recurring failures directly weaken the premium proposition.

Management has shortened product-development cycles from 18-24 months to 15-16 months, and they’re targeting 12-14 months. That should improve responsiveness, but creates tension between speed and quality. The risk is they’ll miss with new products faster. :) Key metrics to watch here are are women’s comps, leggings growth, markdowns and new-product reception.

Alo, Vuori And Existence of Lock-In

Competition increasingly exposes how little customer lock-in truly exists. Third-party estimates suggest Lululemon lost substantial athleisure share while Alo and Vuori gained. That’s not a coincidence.

Defending share requires better products, heavier marketing or more promotions. And all of that costs money in a way of higher investment, SG&A or lower gross margins. Competitive pressure therefore threatens both growth and Lululemon’s historical margin structure.

China Is Not the Guaranteed Escape Route Anymore

China had been the obvious answer to slowing Americas growth and for quite some time the main counter-argument of bulls towards bears’ scepticism of decline in Americas.

Q1 FY2026 was strong, but Q2 constant-currency revenue fell 2% and comps dropped 8%, despite reported growth supported by store openings. One weak quarter, partly affected by marketing backlash, proves little. It is a risk factor nevertheless and persistent negative comps would weaken a major pillar of the bull case.

Leadership & Turnaround Risk

Heidi O’Neill needs to try to catch a knife that’s falling, turn it around and stab competition with it. She’s inheriting falling Americas traffic, inconsistent product execution, slowing China momentum and a cost base built for growth. Her Nike background is credible, but not a guarantee of success. Excessively conservative guidance would also risk obscuring whether the underlying turnaround is actually working. So, will she grab the knife correctly or get cut nastily?

Share

Financial & Operating-Leverage Risks

The Cost Base Built for Growth

We believe this is the biggest risk in this category. In Q2, SG&A rose 5.7% despite revenue falling 4%, reaching 41.7% of sales. Lululemon ended the quarter with 825 stores and 11% more square footage YoY, while lease liabilities reached $2.14B. Management still expects 10% square-footage growth in FY2026.

That infrastructure is positive and creates leverage when comps rise. BUT, it can become a negative quite quickly when it starts to create brutal reverse leverage when the comps fall. Q3 guidance illustrates this. Revenue down 10-11% and operating margin around 6.5% versus 17% last year.

Markdowns & Capital Allocation

Markdowns increased 70 bps in Q2 and are expected to remain elevated. If customers learn to wait for discounts, Lululemon’s historically high full-price margin structure could reset lower. Inventory itself remains manageable, but prolonged negative comps would worsen the risk.

The balance sheet remains strong, although $695M of H1 buybacks materially exceeded roughly $312M of baseline FCF after capex. Continued buybacks above internal cash generation could reduce flexibility precisely when the turnaround may require more investment, and that would be a really unpleasant situation to find the company in.

Trade, Supply Chain & Macro

Tariffs cost roughly 160 bps of Q2 gross margin excluding the refund. Supply concentration is meaningful, since 40% of finished goods come from Vietnam, 18% from Cambodia, while Taiwan and China supply large portions of fabrics. Taiwan disruption remains low-probability but high-impact.

Macro weakness is important but it doesn’t explain as much variance of Lulu’s downfall as bulls would wish for, as well as it cannot fully explain competitors gaining share. A recession ends at some point. Lost consumer preference may not.

Legal & Technology Risks

Litigation, tax disputes, cybersecurity, AI and more remain secondary risks.

The current problem remains much simpler… Customers are buying less Lululemon.

Our Scenarios (3-5 Year Horizon): Bull, Base, Bear Case

We use a 3-to-5-year horizon to assess whether Lululemon can stabilise North America, restore product relevance and recover part of its historical margin structure. These aren’t estimates of intrinsic value today, but potential future share prices if each operating scenario materialises. Our reference price is the September 4, 2026 close of $100.61.

Bull Case (20% Probability)

Key Assumptions

The current weakness proves primarily a product-cycle problem rather than structural brand erosion. Americas comps recover, international growth re-gains the healthy momentum, markdown pressure normalises and operating margins recover toward 18-19%. Strong FCF and continued buybacks support further EPS growth.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $12.5B in 2029 and $14.5B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $14.50 and $18. Applying multiples of 18x and 17x produces estimated share prices of approximately $260 in 3 years and $305 in 5 years.

From $100.61, that represents annualised returns of approximately 37% and 25%.

Base Case (55% Probability)

Key Assumptions

Lululemon stabilises but doesn’t regain its former dominance. North American growth returns gradually, competitors retain some share and international expansion becomes a less powerful offset. Margins recover from current depressed levels but settle structurally below historical peaks, with operating margins around the mid-teens.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $11.2B in 2029 and $12B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $10.50 and $12. Applying a 14x multiple produces estimated share prices of approximately $150 in 3 years and $170 in 5 years.

From $100.61, that represents annualised returns of approximately 14% and 11%.

Bear Case (25% Probability)

Key Assumptions

The Americas decline proves substantially structural. Lululemon continues losing relevance to premium competitors, international growth increasingly depends on new-store expansion and markdowns and higher marketing spending permanently reduce profitability. Operating margins fall toward the low teens and the market increasingly values Lululemon as a mature apparel retailer.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $9.8B in 2029 and $10.2B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $6.50 and $7.50. Applying multiples of 10x and 10x produces estimated share prices of approximately $65 in 3 years and $75 in 5 years.

From $100.61, that represents annualised returns of approximately -14% and -6%.

Conclusion

Lululemon is no longer the easy compounder it once appeared to be. Americas comps are collapsing, product execution has weakened, competition is rising and margins are under pressure. Yet this isn’t a distressed retailer at least financially-wise. The balance sheet is excellent, FCF remains meaningful, shares are shrinking and international potential remains. At around $100, LULU trades near 10x depressed FY2026 earnings. The opportunity is obvious. But it’s obvious only if today’s problems prove cyclical rather than structural.

The investment case thus comes down to one question:

Is Lululemon experiencing a repairable product and merchandising cycle, or has its preference-based moat structurally weakened?

We believe the answer is probably somewhere in between, and while Dr. Burry clearly strongly believes in the first case, we tend to lean on the side of the second one.

Share

Final Verdict: HOLD

At approximately $100, we rate Lululemon a HOLD.

Valuation is no longer the main issue in LULU investment thesis. At around $100 per share, we understand the Moderate Buy case for investors convinced the weakness is cyclical and new CEO can restore growth and margins. We’re simply not there yet.

Traffic, comps, productivity and margins are still deteriorating and are facts presented to us, while the turnaround remains hypothetical. We’d become more interested if Americas comps stabilise, new products gain traction and margins recover while sentiment remains somewhat negative.

That would fit the Hated Moats philosophy far better than trying to catch the exact bottom, only to realise we’re catching a falling knife.

Hated? For sure. Moat? We’ll need to see about that...
